name: Chinstrap beard

lead: The chinstrap beard is a narrow, continuous strip of hair that runs along the jawline and connects the sideburns beneath the chin, with the cheeks and upper lip clean-shaven. By tracing the lower edge of the jaw, it draws attention to the jawline and can make the lower face look more defined.

Grokipedia describes it as suited to round faces, where the thin line adds angularity, and to square faces, where it traces existing structure. The style has a long history in Europe and America and has returned in waves, including in 2010s hip-hop and sports culture.

paras: Wearers grow facial hair along the jaw and keep it narrow, commonly around 1 to 2 cm, trimming the cheeks and neck clean to give a sharp border. Straight or wavy growth tends to make an even line easier, while curlier hair needs more frequent trimming [1].

It is a grooming style with no health risks beyond routine razor irritation or ingrown hairs. It requires upkeep to keep the line crisp, and opinions on it vary: some forum members have described it as dated or a style that invites mockery.

angle.text: The strap traces the jaw, which proponents say adds visible definition and angularity, especially to rounder faces. It works through grooming rather than any change in bone or tissue.

lead: A chinstrap beard is a facial hair style in which a thin, even band of hair follows the jawline from the sideburns around the chin, leaving the cheeks and usually the upper lip shaved [1]. It is also called a chin curtain or fringe beard [1].

For people trying to improve their look, the style is used to outline the jaw: the line makes a rounder lower face appear more angular and a strong jaw appear more sharply drawn [1]. Grokipedia gives a typical width of roughly 0.4 to 0.8 inches and ties its flattering effect to face shape and hair texture [1].

Wikipedia's broader history of facial hair reports that most men wore some facial hair in the mid-to-late 1800s, with beards peaking around the 1880s before declining [2]. Grokipedia places the chinstrap's popularity in the 1850s and 1860s and notes later revivals [1]. Men on strength-training forums have discussed it informally, including as an option for those whose beards grow patchily [3][4].
infobox: Regular trimming of cheeks and neck

paras: The style is a narrow strip of hair joining the sideburns under the chin, without a mustache or cheek hair, following the line of the mandible [1]. It resembles a goatee in outlining the chin but without the concentration of hair on the chin itself [1].

Grokipedia says the strap suits round faces by introducing angularity, enhances jawline definition on square faces, and balances longer faces by framing the lower face [1]. It adds that straight or wavy facial hair forms the cleanest line and curly hair requires more trimming [1].

Grokipedia describes the style as emerging in 19th-century Europe and spreading to the United States around the Civil War, associating it with public figures such as Abraham Lincoln and Count Cavour, and describing a revival in the 2000s and 2010s [1]. Wikipedia reports that Lincoln is said to have grown his beard on the advice of an 11-year-old girl, Grace Bedell, and that beard prevalence peaked in the 1880s [2].

Posters on T Nation have asked for the community's view on the chinstrap, with one thread asking whether it is seen as 'douchey' or 'awesome' [3], and others have mentioned growing only the chinstrap when the rest of the beard fills in patchily [4].

lore.intro: Forum discussion of the chinstrap is mostly stylistic and humorous, weighing it against fuller beards and mustaches [3][4].
